scenes.title: M32-001
lines: Watch track editing in Super Mario Maker 2. Angular sections become rounded corners and join into a loop. What numbers would make a curved shape easy to control? We will build our own Bezier curve using control points outside the path, then split the same curve into the portions we need.

scenes.title: M32-002
lines: A cubic Bézier curve has four control points. The curve starts at the first point and ends at the last. The two interior points need not lie on its path. Those are shape handles. This is approximation rather than a requirement to interpolate every control point.

scenes.title: M32-003
lines: The construction begins with linear interpolation. To move a fraction t between two points, multiply the first by one minus t, the next by t, and add. Applying the same fraction to adjacent pairs of four controls produces three points, then two, then one.

scenes.title: M32-004
lines: The last point is the curve position at t. As t moves from zero to one, that point traces the curve. Arrange the computation in a triangle: original controls on top, with each lower entry blending the two immediately above. This is de Casteljau's algorithm.

scenes.title: M32-005
lines: The code can overwrite a single array with each row of the triangle. Blend each point with the next, working from left to right, then reduce the active count by one. Repeat until one remains. Here n means the number of points, not the degree. Use a copy if the original controls are needed, and reject an empty array.

scenes.title: M32-006
lines: Expanding the blends gives a polynomial. With two controls it is the first point plus t times their difference. With three, the constant is the first point, the linear coefficient is twice the second minus twice the first, and the quadratic coefficient is first minus twice second plus third. We have grouped the same geometric calculation by powers of t.

scenes.title: M32-007
lines: Put the controls in columns of B. Multiplying by the basis-conversion matrix M gives the power coefficients. Compute those once for repeated evaluations, or multiply M by the powers of t first to obtain control-point weights. Both evaluate the same curve.

scenes.title: M32-008
lines: One more blend yields four cubic coefficients. The constant is b zero. The linear term is three times the difference b one minus b zero. The next coefficient is three times the difference of successive edges, with weights 3, −6, 3. The last coefficient has alternating signs: subtract the first point, add three times the second, subtract three times the third and add the endpoint. Follow each coefficient back to the contributing controls.

scenes.title: M32-009
lines: The conversion also works backward. The first control is c zero; the next is c zero plus one third c one. The second interior control adds two thirds c one and one third c two to c zero. The endpoint sums all coefficients. For a fixed degree representation, these controls are uniquely determined.

scenes.title: M32-010
lines: Let's locate the midpoint in parameter space on this same curve. Set progress to half and mark the midpoint of each neighbouring pair of controls. Repeat with those midpoints until only one point remains. The point sits below the two raised handles. The picture shows that handles draw the curve towards them without making it pass through them.

scenes.title: M32-011
lines: Hold t at one half and move only the first interior handle upward. The endpoints remain fixed, while the departure direction and the interior change. To quantify that influence, regroup the polynomial by control point rather than by powers of t.

scenes.title: M32-012
lines: For two controls, the weights are one minus t and t. With three they become the square of one minus t, two t times one minus t, and t squared. The middle control has two contributing paths, creating the factor two. At cubic degree the coefficients similarly become one, three, three, one.

scenes.title: M32-013
lines: Higher degrees produce Pascal's triangle: ones on the edges, and each interior number the sum of the two above. The degree-four row, one four six four one, supplies quartic coefficients. These binomial coefficients count selections of i items from n, and are computed using factorials. A factorial multiplies all positive integers up to that number; zero factorial is one. Divide n factorial by the product of i factorial and the factorial of n minus i.

scenes.title: M32-014
lines: Each weight is a binomial coefficient times t to the i times one minus t to the n minus i. These are Bernstein basis functions. Multiply every control by its corresponding weight and sum them to evaluate the Bézier curve. At the midpoint of a cubic, the four weights are in the ratio one, three, three, one. Divide each by their sum of eight. Each inner control therefore contributes three times as much as each endpoint.

scenes.title: M32-015
lines: The Bernstein weights sum to one: the binomial theorem makes their sum the nth power of the quantity t plus one minus t. The quantity inside is one, so the result is one. On zero through one they are also nonnegative, keeping the curve inside the controls' convex hull, like a taut rubber band around planar control points. At either end, only the corresponding endpoint weight is one, so the curve interpolates its endpoints.

scenes.title: M32-016
lines: Inside the parameter interval, every weight is positive, so moving one control affects the whole segment. That is global support. Editing only a neighborhood requires local support. A single polynomial cannot vanish throughout an open interval and remain nonzero elsewhere. This motivates joining polynomial pieces into a spline.

scenes.title: M32-017
lines: The weight for control i reaches its maximum at t equal to i over n. For the first interior control of a cubic, its influence peaks at one third. This is closeness in parameter order, not a rule that the spatially nearest control must have the greatest weight.

scenes.title: M32-018
lines: Recall Mario launching toward another planet in Super Mario Galaxy. A path is shaped not only by its destination, but also by the direction in which it begins. In our Bezier construction, the handles let us specify that direction. Now calculate departure direction. Differentiate the power form and substitute zero: the starting derivative is three times the difference b one minus b zero. At the end it is three times the difference between b three and b two. The curve departs toward the first interior control and arrives in the direction from the last interior control toward the endpoint.

scenes.title: M32-019
lines: This directly converts Bézier to Hermite form: keep the endpoints and use the derivatives just calculated. In reverse, add one third of the starting derivative to the start for the first handle, and subtract one third of the ending derivative from the end for the last handle. The curve stays unchanged; only its controls are represented differently.

scenes.title: M32-020
lines: Endpoint acceleration uses the nearest three controls. At the start, subtract twice b one from b zero, add b two, then multiply that whole result by six. If consecutive control-polygon edges are d zero and d one, this is six times the difference between d one and d zero. The endpoint uses the final two edges likewise. Position needs one point, the first derivative two, and the second derivative three.

scenes.title: M32-021
lines: Moving a nearby handle changes an endpoint derivative without moving the endpoint. Controls farther inward preserve lower-order endpoint conditions while affecting higher derivatives. Four equally spaced collinear controls give constant-speed travel along a line. Place the inner controls on their adjacent endpoints instead, and the same line gets smoothstep motion: start at rest and finish at rest.

scenes.title: M32-022
lines: Acceleration is not the same as curvature. Speeding up along a straight line produces acceleration but zero curvature. Traveling around a circle at constant speed produces acceleration because direction changes. Curvature uses the cross-product magnitude divided by speed cubed; the formula is not directly evaluated at zero-speed endpoints.

scenes.title: M32-023
lines: In Satisfactory, rail sections are previewed and connected one at a time. If we want to work on just part of our long curve, we first need to represent that portion as a curve in its own right. Suppose the path is almost right but one region needs finer control. Splitting it gives extra handles where needed. Subdivision also supports adaptive line approximation, using more pieces in curved regions. The goal is not merely to hide part of the old curve, but to produce independent controls describing the same portion.

scenes.title: M32-024
lines: Map the original interval a through b to a new parameter s from zero through one. First find the interval width, b minus a. Multiply that width by s, then add a to obtain t. Zero maps to a and one to b. Substitute this expression into the original polynomial and regroup by powers of s to obtain an independent polynomial for that section. This is reparameterization.

scenes.title: M32-025
lines: To extract a piece of an existing path, map its new progress parameter onto the original one. Put start and end marks on the original curve and sweep new progress from zero to one. The moving point visits only that interval. Multiply new progress by the interval width and add its original start. Substituting that parameter into the position function preserves the selected shape.

scenes.title: M32-026
lines: For a Bézier curve the de Casteljau construction provides that piece directly. Mark the split parameter and interpolate neighbouring control points in that ratio. The last point is the split point on the curve. Follow one edge of the triangle to collect the controls for the left curve. Then follow the other edge for the controls of the right curve. The two curves meet at the split point we just found.

scenes.title: M32-027
lines: The piece keeps its shape, while its playback rate depends on how it is parameterized. Part of the original parameter range now spans zero to one on the new parameter. The new derivative points in the original direction but scales by the original interval width. Comparing physical velocity also requires the chosen duration.

scenes.title: M32-028
lines: Splitting exactly halfway makes the construction easy to see. Mark the midpoint of each neighbouring pair, then take midpoints between those new points. The final midpoint is the endpoint shared by the two pieces. Their differently coloured handles generate pieces that together coincide with the original curve.

scenes.title: M32-029
lines: Select an arbitrary subinterval instead of simply splitting at the midpoint. Denote its start by a and its end by b. For a cubic we interpolate three times. Use the start three times at the first control, twice with one end at the second, once with two ends at the third, and the end three times at the last control. Their order does not matter in exact arithmetic—only their multiplicities. This symmetric multiaffine representation is called blossoming.

scenes.title: M32-030
lines: We began by looking for inputs that make a curve easy to control. Repeated interpolation produced the point; weights and derivatives explained the handles. Collecting the same intermediate points let us split the curve without changing its shape. The remaining question is how to join multiple pieces smoothly.
